## 1. Spec

Turn the intent into `spec.md`, the design an engineer builds from. No
code. Start from how the system works today (`docs/architecture.md` and the
code) and describe the change against it: the new and changed rules; the
API changes, with request and response examples and every new error; how
the server enforces the rules without keeping state; the page (what shows
when, keyboard and screen-reader use, small screens); which modules change
and how; what must keep working exactly as before; and how each line of the
intent's "How we will know it worked" and "What must not change" will be
checked. End with **Open questions**: each one gets the decision you took,
so nothing blocks the next phase.

## 2. Plan

Turn `spec.md` into `plan.md`, an implementation plan. No code. The first
line is `# Plan: <title>`. Then 2 to 4 phases, each a heading
`## Phase N: <name>` followed only by task lines `- [ ] <task>`, 3 to 6
tasks each. Each phase ends with a task that verifies it by running
something, and leaves the game working. Verification uses what every
session has: `python3` (the tests, a throwaway script, a server started
with `--port 0` and driven with `urllib`) and `ruff`. No browser and no
other tools: how the page looks and feels is checked by a person at the
preview after phase 3, so list those checks under a final heading
`## For the preview` as plain bullets, not boxes. Writing new tests is
phase 4 of this process, not part of this plan, but the existing tests
must keep passing after every phase.

## 3. Implement

Implement the first phase of `plan.md` that still has unchecked boxes, and
only that phase. Tick each box (`- [ ]` to `- [x]`) as soon as its task is
done, one edit per task. Follow `spec.md`. If you must depart from it,
update `spec.md` so the two agree. Keep `docs/architecture.md` true. Do not
write new tests yet, but run the existing ones. If a verify task asks for
something you cannot run, do the part you can, tick it, and add what is
left to `## For the preview`.

## Preview (done by a person)

A person runs the change on a preview server, goes through
`## For the preview`, and records the result in `preview.md`: who, when,
and what passed or failed. That file is the sign-off for everything only a
browser can show. Later phases read it; they do not repeat those checks.

## 4. Unit tests

Write pytest tests in `tests/` for every rule in `spec.md`, next to the
existing ones: every new rule, every new error, and every "must not change"
promise of the intent. Call the code directly, not over the network. Run
the whole suite. If a test finds a bug, fix the code and say so in your
final message.

## 5. System test

Test the real system from the outside, extending `tests/system/`: start
`python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` as a process and, over HTTP, play the new
feature end to end, including the attempts the intent says must fail, and
show that the old game still behaves as before. Always stop the server,
even when a test fails. Run the whole suite. Write `test-report.md`: what
was tested, the result, and any bugs found and fixed.

## 6. Lint

Run `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .`. Fix every finding in the
code, run the tests again, and stop when both are clean and the tests pass.
Never silence a finding (see `CLAUDE.md`).

## 7. Code review

Act as a reviewer who did not write this change. Read the intent, the spec,
the diff of the change (`git diff` against the commit before its spec) and
the code around it. Look for: bugs; gaps between intent, spec, code and
`docs/architecture.md`; rules that are not tested; security (the server
faces the internet and trusts no request); and accessibility. The browser
checks belong to `preview.md`: a problem it reports is a finding, but how
much a sign-off is worth (who looked, how closely) is for whoever releases
to judge, so say it in the verdict, not as a finding. Do not change any
code. Write `review.md`: one line per finding,

```markdown
- [ ] **blocker|major|minor** `path:line`: what is wrong, and why it matters
```

most severe first, then a one-paragraph verdict. If there is nothing to

are cheap. Tick each finding as you fix it. Leave a finding you decide not
to fix unticked, with the reason after it. Add a test for every bug you
fix. Finish with the tests and lint clean.

## 9. Deploy

Follow `docs/deploy.md`.

# Intent: a secret cheat code

*From: Product. For: the games team. Change name: `cheat-code`.*

## Why

Tic-tac-toe has been live for a month. People play, but Hard can never be
beaten, and many players quit after two or three draws. Players love
secrets they can share with friends: we want a hidden cheat code that lets
you beat the computer once in a while. Players will pass the code around,
which brings them back to the page and brings their friends.

## What we want

- A secret code typed on the keyboard during a game against the computer
  unlocks a cheat for that game: the player may **steal** one square from
  the computer. The computer's mark on that square becomes the player's
  mark, and that counts as the player's move.
- One steal per game. It is never shown or hinted at on the page until the
  code has been typed. After that, the page makes clear how to use it.
- The code is the classic one: up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right,
  B, A.
- A game won with a steal is announced differently ("You won... with a
  little help"), and it is counted separately in the score. It must not
  count as a normal win.
- The cheat works only against the computer, at both levels, and not when
  two friends play on the same screen.

## What must not change

- Without the code, the game behaves exactly as it does today, and Hard
  still never loses to fair play.
- On the page, nobody can steal without typing the code. Nobody can steal
  twice in a game, even by sending requests to the server by hand.

## How we will know it worked

- It is live in production, the old game unchanged.
- People share the code: we see steals in games we did not set up ourselves.
# Spec: a secret cheat code (`cheat-code`)

Source: `changes/cheat-code/intent.md`. This is the design to build from.
It describes the change against the system as it is today
(`docs/architecture.md`, `tictactoe/`).

## Summary

Against the computer, typing ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A on the page unlocks a
**steal** for the current game: once per game the player may turn one of
the computer's O squares into an X, and that is the player's move. A win
that used a steal is announced as "You won... with a little help" and
counted in its own score column, never as a normal win.

The browser recognises the code and shows the steal controls. The server
judges every steal. To enforce "one steal per game" without keeping state,
the server signs each game position it hands out (an HMAC **game token**)
and accepts a steal only together with a valid token that says no steal has
been used. Requests without a token behave exactly as today.

## How it works today (the parts this change touches)

- A board is 9 cells, `"X"`, `"O"` or `""`. Whose turn it is follows from
  the counts: `game.turn()` is X when X count == O count. `game.validate()`
  accepts a board only if X count − O count is 0 or 1.
- `POST /api/move` takes the whole board, `cell`, `mode`, `level`. Against
  the computer the player is X and the board must have X to move. The server
  plays `cell`, then the computer's reply, and answers the new board.
- The server trusts nothing: any board that passes `validate()` is accepted.
  It has no idea whether that board came from a real game.
- The score (X wins, O wins, draws) lives in `app.js` until reload.

## New and changed rules

1. **Steal.** In a game against the computer, on the player's turn (X to
   move, game still playing), the player may name one cell that holds `"O"`.
   That cell becomes `"X"`. This is the player's move: the computer then
   replies as usual if the game goes on.
2. **Once per game.** A game has at most one steal. A game is one unbroken
   chain of positions handed out by the server, starting from the empty
   board (see "Game token").
3. **Only against the computer**, at both levels (`easy`, `hard`). Never in
   `friend` mode.
4. **Turn after a steal.** A steal changes a mark without adding one, so the
   counts no longer say whose turn it is. The rule becomes: with `s` steals
   used in the game (0 or 1), X is to move when X count − O count == `s`,
   otherwise O. A valid board has X count − O count equal to `s` or `s + 1`.
   With `s = 0` both rules are exactly today's.
5. **A steal can win at once.** If the stolen square completes a line of X,
   the game is won by X and the computer does not move. A steal never fills
   an empty square, so it cannot cause a draw by itself.
6. **Assisted win.** A game won by X in which a steal was used is an
   *assisted* win. The server says so in every answer (`assisted: true`).
   The page announces it as "You won... with a little help" and counts it
   only in the "With help" column, not in "X wins".
7. After a steal the game goes on normally: the computer (either level)
   plays its best/random move from the new position, and the computer can
   still win or draw. Those are counted as today (O win, draw).
8. **The code.** ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A (`ArrowUp ArrowUp ArrowDown ArrowDown
   ArrowLeft ArrowRight ArrowLeft ArrowRight b a`, B and A in either case).
   The code is recognised by the page only; it unlocks the steal controls
   for the current game. The server does not check the code (see Open
   questions 1).

## Game token (how the server enforces the rules without state)

The server keeps nothing between requests. Instead it signs what it must
trust when the browser sends it back, as `CLAUDE.md` allows.

- **Key.** `TICTACTOE_SECRET` from the environment (UTF-8 bytes) when set
  and not empty; otherwise 32 random bytes from `secrets.token_bytes` made
  once when the process starts. Production sets it through `ops/deploy.sh`
  and keeps it across releases, so tokens survive a deploy. The key is
  never logged, never sent, never put in an error message.
- **Format.** `"<s>.<mac>"`, where `<s>` is the number of steals used (`0`
  or `1`) and `<mac>` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the message
  `tictactoe-game-v1|<level>|<s>|<cells>`, with `<cells>` the 9 cells, each
  written as `X`, `O` or `-`. Example: `"0.3f9a…c1"` (64 hex digits).
  The token binds the board, the level and the steal count together;
  change any of them and it no longer verifies.
- **Checking.** Compare with `hmac.compare_digest`. A token that is not a
  string, has the wrong shape, an `<s>` other than `0`/`1`, or a MAC that
  does not match the request's `board` and `level` is rejected with
  `400 {"error": "the game token does not match this game"}`. This applies
  to any request that carries a `game` field, steal or not.
- **When the server hands one out** (the `game` field of the answer), only
  in `computer` mode and only while the game is still `playing`:
  - the request carried a valid token: the new position gets a token with
    the same `s` (or `s = 1` if this request was the steal);
  - the request had no token and its board was empty (first move of a new
    game): the new position gets a token with `s = 0`;
  - otherwise (no token, board not empty, e.g. a hand-made mid-game board
    or an older page): `game` is `null`. That game plays exactly as today
    and can never steal.
  So a token proves that the position was reached by legal moves through
  this server from an empty board, with `s` steals on the way.
- **Why this stops a second steal, even by hand.** A steal needs a token
  with `s = 0`. The answer to a steal only ever carries `s = 1` tokens, and
  every later answer in that game keeps `s = 1`. A board that has had a
  steal has X − O == 1 on X's turn, which no `s = 0` token can match and
  which `validate()` rejects without a token. Forging an `s = 0` token
  needs the key.
- **Replays.** Because the server is stateless, an old token stays valid.
  A player who kept an `s = 0` token from earlier in the same game can go
  back to that position and steal from there. That is a branch of the game
  (like an undo), and every branch still has at most one steal. Accepted
  (Open questions 3).

## API changes

`POST /api/move` keeps its path, limits (1024-byte body, 411, 413, 404,
405) and every existing field and error. New, all optional in the request:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `steal` | A cell 0–8 to steal, sent **instead of** `cell`. |
| `game` | The `game` token from the server's previous answer. |

New in every `200` answer (all modes):

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `game` | Token for the new position, or `null` (rules above). |
| `stealable` | Cells the player could steal now: the O cells when this answer has a token with `s = 0`, the game is playing and X is to move; otherwise `[]`. |
| `steal_used` | `true` once a steal has been used in this game (`s = 1`), else `false`. |
| `assisted` | `true` when `status` is `won`, `winner` is `X` and `steal_used` is `true`; else `false`. |

The page uses `stealable`, `steal_used` and `assisted` as given; it never
works out for itself which squares can be stolen or whether a win was
assisted.

### Examples (Hard; tokens shortened)

First move of a new game, no token (the existing request, unchanged):

```json
{"board": ["", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", ""], "cell": 0, "mode": "computer", "level": "hard"}
```

```json
{"board": ["X", "", "", "", "O", "", "", "", ""], "status": "playing",
 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 4,
 "game": "0.<64 hex>", "stealable": [4], "steal_used": false, "assisted": false}
```

Next move, sending the token back:

```json
{"board": ["X", "", "", "", "O", "", "", "", ""], "cell": 8, "mode": "computer",
 "level": "hard", "game": "0.<64 hex>"}
```

```json
{"board": ["X", "O", "", "", "O", "", "", "", "X"], "status": "playing",
 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 1,
 "game": "0.<64 hex>", "stealable": [1, 4], "steal_used": false, "assisted": false}
```

The steal: taking the centre completes the diagonal 0-4-8.

```json
{"board": ["X", "O", "", "", "O", "", "", "", "X"], "steal": 4, "mode": "computer",
 "level": "hard", "game": "0.<64 hex>"}
```

```json
{"board": ["X", "O", "", "", "X", "", "", "", "X"], "status": "won",
 "winner": "X", "line": [0, 4, 8], "turn": null, "computer_move": null,
 "game": null, "stealable": [], "steal_used": true, "assisted": true}
```

A steal that does not win (stealing cell 1 instead) gets the computer's
reply and an `s = 1` token; X is to move with X − O == 1. (Hard must block
row 0 at cell 2; this reply is the expected one, not recorded from code.)

```json
{"board": ["X", "X", "O", "", "O", "", "", "", "X"], "status": "playing",
 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 2,
 "game": "1.<64 hex>", "stealable": [], "steal_used": true, "assisted": false}
```

A friend game answers `game: null, stealable: [], steal_used: false,
assisted: false` in addition to today's fields.

### New errors (all `400 {"error": "..."}`)

Checked in this order, after today's checks of the body, `board` shape,
`mode` and `level`:

| Case | Message |
|------|---------|
| `game` present but not valid for this `board` and `level` (any request) | `the game token does not match this game` |
| both `cell` and `steal` present | `send either cell or steal, not both` |
| `steal` in `friend` mode | `you can only steal from the computer` |
| `steal` without `game` | `a steal needs the game token from the last answer` |
| `steal` with a token whose `s` is 1 | `you have already stolen a square in this game` |
| `steal` not a whole number 0–8 (`true` is not a number) | `steal must be a whole number from 0 to 8` |
| game already over | `the game is over` (today's message) |
| the cell is not an O (empty or X) | `you can only steal one of the computer's squares` |

The board check uses the token's `s`: a board with X − O outside
`s`..`s + 1` is rejected with today's message `X moves first and the
players alternate`, and with X − O ≠ `s` against the computer with today's
`against the computer you play X`.

## Logging (to see steals in production)

The intent will judge success by steals in games "we did not set up". The
server has no database, so after every successful steal the request handler
writes one line through `log_message` (stderr, which `ops/deploy.sh` sends
to `production/server.log`, next to the request line with the client
address):

```text
steal level=hard cell=4 status=won assisted=true
```

Nothing else is logged: no token, no key, no board. Because a steal needs a
token chain that started from an empty board, every logged steal happened
in a real game played through the server.

## The page

### Before the code (unchanged)

The page looks and behaves exactly as today: no steal button, no hint, no
"With help" column, no change to labels or status texts. The new elements
exist in `index.html` with `hidden` and are not shown or announced.

### Recognising the code

- `app.js` listens to `keydown` on `document` and keeps the last 10 keys.
  When they equal the code, the code is typed. A sliding window means extra
  keys before it do not matter (↑ ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ … still works).
- Ignored: events with Ctrl, Alt or Meta held, and auto-repeat
  (`event.repeat`). Keys typed while focus is in a `<select>` are not
  recorded (arrows there change the mode or level, which starts a new game).
- The board's own arrow handling stays as it is: typing the code with the
  focus on the board moves the focus around, which is harmless; arrows never
  play a move.
- The code unlocks only when the mode is `computer` and the game is
  `playing`. Otherwise it does nothing at all (friend mode: no message, no
  hint).
- Unlocking lasts for the current game. A new game (button, mode or level
  change) locks it again; typing the code again unlocks it again.

### After the code

- The status line (`aria-live`) announces: "Cheat unlocked! Once this game,
  you may steal one of the computer's squares." The current status text
  follows after the next move as usual.
- A panel under the status line appears with a **Steal a square** button
  (`aria-pressed`) and the short text "Press Steal, then choose an O. Esc
  cancels." The button is disabled-looking (`aria-disabled="true"`, still
  focusable) when `stealable` is empty, with the reason in the panel text:
  "No O to steal yet" before the computer has moved, "Steal used" after.
- The score table shows a fourth column **With help** (and keeps showing it
  until the page is reloaded, so the count stays visible).

### Steal mode

- Pressing the button (click, Enter, Space) turns steal mode on, but only
  if `stealable` is not empty. The status line says "Steal: choose one of
  the computer's squares." The focus moves to the lowest stealable square
  (roving `tabindex` as today).
- In steal mode only the squares in `stealable` are active
  (`aria-disabled="false"`, class `stealable` with a visible dashed outline
  that does not rely on colour alone). Their label gains ", can be stolen",
  e.g. "Row 2, column 2, O, can be stolen". Every other square is
  `aria-disabled="true"` and does nothing when chosen.
- Choosing a stealable square (click, tap, Enter, Space) sends
  `{board, steal, mode, level, game}`. Steal mode ends with the answer.
- Esc, or pressing the button again, ends steal mode without a move and
  puts the focus back on the button.
- Outside steal mode, clicking an O does nothing, as today.

### After a steal

- The status line says "You stole row R, column C." when the game goes on
  (then the usual "Your turn (X)" on the next render), and "You won... with
  a little help" when the steal or a later move wins with `assisted: true`.
- Score: `assisted: true` adds 1 to **With help** and nothing to X wins.
  A computer win or a draw after a steal counts as today.
- The panel says "Steal used" and the button stays disabled-looking.

### Small screens

The panel and the four-column score table must fit 320 px wide with no
horizontal scroll: the column headings are short ("X wins", "O wins",
"Draws", "With help") and the button is at least 44 px tall. The code
needs a keyboard, so phones without one cannot unlock it (Open questions 2).

## Modules

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `game.py` | `turn(board, steals=0)`, `validate(board, steals=0)`, `play(board, cell, steals=0)` follow rule 4. ## Open questions (with the decision taken)

1. **Should the server check the code?** No. The code is meant to be
   shared, so anyone sending requests by hand knows it anyway; making the
   browser send it would add nothing. "Nobody can steal without the code"
   is a promise about the page, kept by the page. The server enforces what
   it can: computer mode only, a real game, at most one steal.
2. **Phones and tablets without a keyboard?** Out of scope: the intent says
   "typed on the keyboard". No touch gesture is added. Product can ask for
   one as a separate change.
3. **Replaying an older token to steal in a different branch of the same
   game?** Allowed: it cannot be stopped without server state, and each
   branch still has at most one steal. Equivalent to starting over and
   replaying the same moves.
4. **Tokens for games already running when this ships?** Those pages run
   the old `app.js` and never send `game`; they play on as today and cannot
   steal. After a reload they get tokens.
5. **Development restarts.** Without `TICTACTOE_SECRET`, a restart makes a
   new key, so a game in progress gets 400 "the game token does not match"

   error and New game fixes it. Production keeps its key across releases.
6. **Is an assisted win also an X win in the API?** Yes: `status: "won"`,
   `winner: "X"` as today, plus `assisted: true`. Only the page's score
   counts it separately. Keeps old clients and `status` unchanged.
7. **Can the computer still win after a steal?** Yes, and that is counted
   as a normal O win; a draw after a steal is a normal draw. Only X wins
   are "with help".
8. **Token after the game ends?** `null`: there is nothing left to play.
9. **Where the code lives in `app.js`.** Plain in the source. It is a
   shared secret by design; hiding it would be theatre.
# tictactoe

Tic-tac-toe for the website's games corner: a drawn 3x3 board in the
browser, against the computer (Easy or Hard, which never loses) or against
a friend on the same screen. The page keeps a running score and can be
played with the keyboard alone.

```bash
python3 -m tictactoe              # http://127.0.0.1:8000/
python3 -m tictactoe --port 0     # any free port; the URL is printed
python3 -m pytest -q              # unit and system tests
ruff check . && ruff format --check .
./ops/deploy.sh                   # to production, see docs/deploy.md
```

184	## How it works today (the parts this change touches)
185	
186	- A board is 9 cells, `"X"`, `"O"` or `""`. Whose turn it is follows from
187	  the counts: `game.turn()` is X when X count == O count. `game.validate()`

198	1. **Steal.** In a game against the computer, on the player's turn (X to
199	   move, game still playing), the player may name one cell that holds `"O"`.
200	   That cell becomes `"X"`. This is the player's move: the computer then

210	   otherwise O. A valid board has X count − O count equal to `s` or `s + 1`.

228	## Game token (how the server enforces the rules without state)
229	
230	The server keeps nothing between requests. Instead it signs what it must
231	trust when the browser sends it back, as `CLAUDE.md` allows.
232	
233	- **Key.** `TICTACTOE_SECRET` from the environment (UTF-8 bytes) when set
234	  and not empty; otherwise 32 random bytes from `secrets.token_bytes` made
235	  once when the process starts. Production sets it through `ops/deploy.sh`
236	  and keeps it across releases, so tokens survive a deploy. The key is
237	  never logged, never sent, never put in an error message.
238	- **Format.** `"<s>.<mac>"`, where `<s>` is the number of steals used (`0`
239	  or `1`) and `<mac>` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the message
240	  `tictactoe-game-v1|<level>|<s>|<cells>`, with `<cells>` the 9 cells, each
241	  written as `X`, `O` or `-`. Example: `"0.3f9a…c1"` (64 hex digits).

243	  change any of them and it no longer verifies.
244	- **Checking.** Compare with `hmac.compare_digest`. A token that is not a
245	  string, has the wrong shape, an `<s>` other than `0`/`1`, or a MAC that

249	- **When the server hands one out** (the `game` field of the answer), only
250	  in `computer` mode and only while the game is still `playing`:

393	### Recognising the code

395	- `app.js` listens to `keydown` on `document` and keeps the last 10 keys.
396	  When they equal the code, the code is typed. A sliding window means extra
397	  keys before it do not matter (↑ ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ … still works).
398	- Ignored: events with Ctrl, Alt or Meta held, and auto-repeat
399	  (`event.repeat`). Keys typed while focus is in a `<select>` are not
400	  recorded (arrows there change the mode or level, which starts a new game).
401	- The board's own arrow handling stays as it is: typing the code with the
402	  focus on the board moves the focus around, which is harmless; arrows never
403	  play a move.
404	- The code unlocks only when the mode is `computer` and the game is
405	  `playing`. Otherwise it does nothing at all (friend mode: no message, no
406	  hint).
407	- Unlocking lasts for the current game. A new game (button, mode or level
408	  change) locks it again; typing the code again unlocks it again.
409	
410	### After the code
411	
412	- The status line (`aria-live`) announces: "Cheat unlocked! Once this game,
413	  you may steal one of the computer's squares." The current status text
414	  follows after the next move as usual.
415	- A panel under the status line appears with a **Steal a square** button
416	  (`aria-pressed`) and the short text "Press Steal, then choose an O. Esc
417	  cancels." The button is disabled-looking (`aria-disabled="true"`, still
418	  focusable) when `stealable` is empty, with the reason in the panel text:
419	  "No O to steal yet" before the computer has moved, "Steal used" after.
420	- The score table shows a fourth column **With help** (and keeps showing it
421	  until the page is reloaded, so the count stays visible).
422	
423	### Steal mode
424	
425	- Pressing the button (click, Enter, Space) turns steal mode on, but only
426	  if `stealable` is not empty. The status line says "Steal: choose one of
427	  the computer's squares." The focus moves to the lowest stealable square
428	  (roving `tabindex` as today).
429	- In steal mode only the squares in `stealable` are active
430	  (`aria-disabled="false"`, class `stealable` with a visible dashed outline
431	  that does not rely on colour alone). Their label gains ", can be stolen",
432	  e.g. "Row 2, column 2, O, can be stolen". Every other square is
433	  `aria-disabled="true"` and does nothing when chosen.
434	- Choosing a stealable square (click, tap, Enter, Space) sends
435	  `{board, steal, mode, level, game}`. Steal mode ends with the answer.
436	- Esc, or pressing the button again, ends steal mode without a move and
437	  puts the focus back on the button.
438	- Outside steal mode, clicking an O does nothing, as today.
439	
440	### After a steal
441	
442	- The status line says "You stole row R, column C." when the game goes on
443	  (then the usual "Your turn (X)" on the next render), and "You won... with
444	  a little help" when the steal or a later move wins with `assisted: true`.
445	- Score: `assisted: true` adds 1 to **With help** and nothing to X wins.
446	  A computer win or a draw after a steal counts as today.
447	- The panel says "Steal used" and the button stays disabled-looking.
448	
449	### Small screens
450	
451	The panel and the four-column score table must fit 320 px wide with no
452	horizontal scroll: the column headings are short ("X wins", "O wins",
453	"Draws", "With help") and the button is at least 44 px tall. The code
454	needs a keyboard, so phones without one cannot unlock it (Open questions 2).
455	
456	## Modules
457	
458	| File | Change |
459	|------|--------|
460	| `game.py` | `turn(board, steals=0)`, `validate(board, steals=0)`, `play(board, cell, steals=0)` follow rule 4. New `steal(board, cell, steals) -> list[str]`: checks and errors from the table above (already stolen, cell type, game over, not X's turn, not an O); returns a new board, never changes its input. `outcome()` and `legal_moves()` do not change. |
461	| `ai.py` | `choose_move(board, level, rng=None, *, steals=0)`; `best_move` and `value` take `steals` too (still cached), so the search uses the right turn after a steal. With `steals=0` the moves are exactly today's. |
462	| new `signing.py` | The key (env or random at import, as above), `sign(board, level, steals) -> str`, `verify(token, board, level) -> int` (returns `s`, raises `IllegalMoveError`). Nothing else imports `os.environ`. |
463	| `server.py` | `handle_move` reads `game` and `steal`, verifies, plays the move or the steal, then the computer's reply with the right `steals`, and adds `game`, `stealable`, `steal_used`, `assisted`. `describe()` takes `steals`. `do_POST` writes the steal log line. Signature `handle_move(request)` stays. |
464	| `static/index.html` | Hidden cheat panel (button + text) under the status line; hidden "With help" column in the score table. |
465	| `static/app.js` | Code recognition, unlock state per game, steal mode, sending `game` back with every move, the new status texts, the fourth score counter. |
466	| `static/style.css` | `.stealable` outline, panel layout, small-screen fit. |
467	| `docs/architecture.md` | Updated in phase 3: the token, the new fields and errors, the turn rule, `signing.py`, the page's cheat. |
468	
469	## What must keep working exactly as before
470	
471	- Every request without `steal` and without `game` gets the same `board`,
472	  `status`, `winner`, `line`, `turn`, `computer_move` and the same errors
473	  as today; the only difference is the four added fields.
474	- Hard is unchanged for `steals=0` and never loses to fair play
475	  (`test_hard_never_loses` passes untouched). Easy is unchanged.
476	- Friend mode, `/health` (`200 ok`), the assets, 404/405/411/413, the
477	  1024-byte limit, the keyboard model of the board and its labels.
478	- All existing tests pass without change.
479	
480	## How each line of the intent will be checked
481	
482	| Intent line | Check |
483	|-------------|-------|
484	| Code unlocks one steal for that game; computer's mark becomes the player's; counts as the move | Unit (`game.steal`, `handle_move`) and system test: play a game over HTTP with tokens, steal, see the cell become X and the computer reply. Preview: type the code, steal with mouse and with keyboard. |
485	| One steal per game | Unit and system: a second steal with the returned token → 400 "already stolen". |
486	| Never shown or hinted at until the code; then clear how to use it | Preview: page before the code is identical to today (no button, no column, no label change); after the code the panel, text and announcement appear. |
487	| The code is ↑↑↓↓←→←→BA | Preview: the exact code unlocks; a wrong key in the middle does not; the sliding window works; uppercase B A works. |
488	| Won with a steal is announced differently and counted separately | Unit/system: `assisted: true` only for X wins with a steal. Preview: "You won... with a little help", "With help" goes up, "X wins" does not. |
489	| Only against the computer, both levels, not friend | Unit/system: steal works at easy and hard; friend → 400. Preview: the code does nothing in friend mode. |
490	| Without the code, exactly as today; Hard never loses to fair play | Existing unit and system tests untouched and passing; new unit test that tokenless answers equal today's fields; `test_hard_never_loses`. |
491	| On the page, nobody can steal without the code | Preview: clicking or pressing Enter on an O does nothing before the code. (The server cannot know about keys; see Open questions 1.) |
492	| Nobody can steal twice, even by hand | Unit and system: second steal → 400; steal without token, with a token for another board, another level, a hand-edited `0.`/`1.` prefix, a malformed token → 400; a hand-made mid-game board without token gets `game: null`. |
493	| Live in production, old game unchanged | Phase 9: `ops/deploy.sh`, then `curl` `/health`, the page, and one tokenless move whose old fields match today's answer. |
494	| We see steals in games we did not set up | The `steal …` log line in `production/server.log`; system test checks the server prints it on a steal and never prints the key or token. After launch, Product reads the log (client addresses are in the request lines). |
495	
496	## Open questions (with the decision taken)
497	
498	1. **Should the server check the code?** No. The code is meant to be
499	   shared, so anyone sending requests by hand knows it anyway; making the
500	   browser send it would add nothing. "Nobody can steal without the code"
501	   is a promise about the page, kept by the page. The server enforces what
502	   it can: computer mode only, a real game, at most one steal.
503	2. **Phones and tablets without a keyboard?** Out of scope: the intent says
504	   "typed on the keyboard". No touch gesture is added. Product can ask for
505	   one as a separate change.
506	3. **Replaying an older token to steal in a different branch of the same
507	   game?** Allowed: it cannot be stopped without server state, and each
508	   branch still has at most one steal. Equivalent to starting over and
509	   replaying the same moves.
510	4. **Tokens for games already running when this ships?** Those pages run
511	   the old `app.js` and never send `game`; they play on as today and cannot
512	   steal. After a reload they get tokens.
513	5. **Development restarts.** Without `TICTACTOE_SECRET`, a restart makes a
514	   new key, so a game in progress gets 400 "the game token does not match"
515	   on its next move. Accepted for development; the page shows its usual
516	   error and New game fixes it. Production keeps its key across releases.
517	6. **Is an assisted win also an X win in the API?** Yes: `status: "won"`,
518	   `winner: "X"` as today, plus `assisted: true`. Only the page's score
519	   counts it separately. Keeps old clients and `status` unchanged.
520	7. **Can the computer still win after a steal?** Yes, and that is counted
521	   as a normal O win; a draw after a steal is a normal draw. Only X wins
522	   are "with help".
523	8. **Token after the game ends?** `null`: there is nothing left to play.
524	9. **Where the code lives in `app.js`.** Plain in the source. It is a
525	   shared secret by design; hiding it would be theatre.
526	# tictactoe
527	
528	Tic-tac-toe for the website's games corner: a drawn 3x3 board in the
529	browser, against the computer (Easy or Hard, which never loses) or against
530	a friend on the same screen. The page keeps a running score and can be
531	played with the keyboard alone.
532	
533	```bash
534	python3 -m tictactoe              # http://127.0.0.1:8000/
535	python3 -m tictactoe --port 0     # any free port; the URL is printed
536	python3 -m pytest -q              # unit and system tests
537	ruff check . && ruff format --check .
538	./ops/deploy.sh                   # to production, see docs/deploy.md
539	```
540	
541	Python 3.12 or newer, standard library only.
542	
543	## Documentation
544	
545	- `docs/architecture.md`: modules, the move API, how the page works
546	- `docs/process.md`: how a change goes from intent to production
547	- `docs/deploy.md`: production and how to deploy to it
548	- `changes/<name>/`: one folder per change, with its intent, spec, plan,
549	  test report and review
550	# Architecture
551	
552	```text
553	browser (static/)                          server (Python, stdlib)
554	┌───────────────────────┐  POST /api/move  ┌────────────────────────────┐
555	│ index.html  app.js    │ ───────────────▶ │ server.py  handle_move()   │
556	│ draws, sends clicks,  │    whole board   │   ├─ game.py  rules        │
557	│ keeps the score       │ ◀─────────────── │   └─ ai.py    computer     │
558	└───────────────────────┘   new board +    └────────────────────────────┘
559	                            outcome
560	```
561	
562	The rules live in Python only. The browser never decides whether a move is
563	legal or who won: it shows what the server answers.
564	
565	## Modules (`tictactoe/`)
566	
567	| File | Job |
568	|------|-----|
569	| `game.py` | The rules. A board is a list of 9 cells, row by row, each `"X"`, `"O"` or `""`. X moves first, so `turn()` follows from the counts. `validate()` checks a board from outside, `play()` returns a new board (never changes its input) or raises `IllegalMoveError`, `outcome()` says `playing`, `won` (with winner and line) or `draw`. |
570	| `ai.py` | The computer. `choose_move(board, level)`: **hard** is negamax over the full game tree, cached, lowest cell among equals, so it is deterministic and never loses; **easy** takes a winning move if it sees one, otherwise plays at random. |
571	| `server.py` | `ThreadingHTTPServer`. Serves a fixed map of assets (no request path reaches the file system), `/health`, and the move API. Keeps no state. |
572	| `__main__.py` | `python3 -m tictactoe [--host] [--port]`; prints the URL it listens on. |
573	| `static/` | `index.html`, `style.css`, `app.js`. No build step, no libraries. |
574	
575	## The move API
576	
577	`POST /api/move`, a JSON body of at most 1024 bytes:
578	
579	```json
580	{"board": ["X", "", "", "", "O", "", "", "", ""], "cell": 2, "mode": "computer", "level": "hard"}
581	```
582	
583	- `mode` is `computer` (default) or `friend`; `level` is `easy` or `hard`
584	  (default), used only against the computer.
585	- Against the computer the player is always X, so the board must have X
586	  to move.
587	- The server plays `cell` for whoever is to move, then, against the
588	  computer and if the game goes on, the computer's reply as O.
589	
590	Answer `200`:
591	
592	```json
593	{"board": ["X", "", "X", "", "O", "", "", "", "O"], "status": "playing",
594	 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 8}
595	```
596	
597	`status` is `playing`, `won` or `draw`; `line` is the three winning cells;
598	`turn` is `null` once the game is over; `computer_move` is `null` when the
599	computer did not move.
600	
601	Errors: `400 {"error": "..."}` for any bad input (bad JSON, impossible
602	board, taken square, game over, unknown mode or level), `411` without a
603	`Content-Length`, `413` for a body over 1024 bytes, `404` for other paths,
604	`405` for `GET /api/move`.
605	
606	## The page
607	
608	`app.js` holds the current answer from the server and the score (X wins, O
609	wins, draws, until the page is reloaded). Each click or Enter/Space on a
610	square sends one move. The board is one tab stop: arrow keys, Home and End
611	move between squares (roving `tabindex`), and every square has an
612	`aria-label` such as "Row 1, column 3, X, winning". The status line is an
613	`aria-live` region. Changing mode or level starts a new game.
614	
615	## Tests
616	
617	- `tests/test_game.py`, `tests/test_ai.py`, `tests/test_server.py`: unit
618	  tests. `test_hard_never_loses` plays Hard against every possible opponent,
619	  as X and as O.
620	- `tests/system/test_http.py`: starts `python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` as a
621	  process and tests it over HTTP: health, assets, 404s, whole games, errors.

# How a change goes from intent to production

A change lives in `changes/<name>/`. The business writes `intent.md` there.
Each phase is done by a fresh session that reads the artifacts of the
earlier phases and leaves its own for the next one. The files are the only
memory, so write each artifact for a reader who was not there. Below,
`<change>` stands for `changes/<name>/`.

| # | Phase | Reads | Leaves |
|---|-------|-------|--------|
| 1 | Spec | `<change>/intent.md`, the code, `docs/` | `<change>/spec.md` |
| 2 | Plan | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `<change>/plan.md` |
| 3 | Implement | `<change>/plan.md`, `<change>/spec.md` | code, `docs/architecture.md` |
| - | Preview (a person) | `## For the preview` in `plan.md` | `<change>/preview.md` |
| 4 | Unit tests | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `tests/` |
| 5 | System test | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `tests/system/`, `<change>/test-report.md` |
| 6 | Lint | the code | clean ruff |
| 7 | Code review | everything | `<change>/review.md` |
| 8 | Review fixes | `<change>/review.md` | fixes, ticked `review.md` |
| 9 | Deploy | `docs/deploy.md` | a release in production |

## 1. Spec

Turn the intent into `spec.md`, the design an engineer builds from. No
code. Start from how the system works today (`docs/architecture.md` and the
code) and describe the change against it: the new and changed rules; the
API changes, with request and response examples and every new error; how
the server enforces the rules without keeping state; the page (what shows
when, keyboard and screen-reader use, small screens); which modules change
and how; what must keep working exactly as before; and how each line of the
intent's "How we will know it worked" and "What must not change" will be
checked. End with **Open questions**: each one gets the decision you took,
so nothing blocks the next phase.

## 2. Plan

Turn `spec.md` into `plan.md`, an implementation plan. No code. The first
line is `# Plan: <title>`. Then 2 to 4 phases, each a heading
`## Phase N: <name>` followed only by task lines `- [ ] <task>`, 3 to 6
tasks each. Each phase ends with a task that verifies it by running
something, and leaves the game working. Verification uses what every
session has: `python3` (the tests, a throwaway script, a server started
with `--port 0` and driven with `urllib`) and `ruff`. No browser and no
other tools: how the page looks and feels is checked by a person at the
preview after phase 3, so list those checks under a final heading
`## For the preview` as plain bullets, not boxes. Writing new tests is
phase 4 of this process, not part of this plan, but the existing tests
must keep passing after every phase.

## 3. Implement

Implement the first phase of `plan.md` that still has unchecked boxes, and
only that phase. Tick each box (`- [ ]` to `- [x]`) as soon as its task is
done, one edit per task. Follow `spec.md`. If you must depart from it,
update `spec.md` so the two agree. Keep `docs/architecture.md` true. Do not
write new tests yet, but run the existing ones. If a verify task asks for
something you cannot run, do the part you can, tick it, and add what is
left to `## For the preview`.

## Preview (done by a person)

A person runs the change on a preview server, goes through
`## For the preview`, and records the result in `preview.md`: who, when,
and what passed or failed. That file is the sign-off for everything only a
browser can show. Later phases read it; they do not repeat those checks.

## 4. Unit tests

Write pytest tests in `tests/` for every rule in `spec.md`, next to the
existing ones: every new rule, every new error, and every "must not change"
promise of the intent. Call the code directly, not over the network. Run
the whole suite. If a test finds a bug, fix the code and say so in your
final message.

## 5. System test

Test the real system from the outside, extending `tests/system/`: start
`python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` as a process and, over HTTP, play the new
feature end to end, including the attempts the intent says must fail, and
show that the old game still behaves as before. Always stop the server,
even when a test fails. Run the whole suite. Write `test-report.md`: what
was tested, the result, and any bugs found and fixed.

## 6. Lint

Run `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .`. Fix every finding in the
code, run the tests again, and stop when both are clean and the tests pass.
Never silence a finding (see `CLAUDE.md`).

## 7. Code review

Act as a reviewer who did not write this change. Read the intent, the spec,
the diff of the change (`git diff` against the commit before its spec) and
the code around it. Look for: bugs; gaps between intent, spec, code and
`docs/architecture.md`; rules that are not tested; security (the server
faces the internet and trusts no request); and accessibility. The browser
checks belong to `preview.md`: a problem it reports is a finding, but how
much a sign-off is worth (who looked, how closely) is for whoever releases
to judge, so say it in the verdict, not as a finding. Do not change any
code. Write `review.md`: one line per finding,

```markdown
- [ ] **blocker|major|minor** `path:line`: what is wrong, and why it matters
```

most severe first, then a one-paragraph verdict. If there is nothing to
report at some severity, say so; do not invent findings.

## 8. Review fixes

Fix every blocker and major finding in `review.md`, and the minors that
are cheap. Tick each finding as you fix it. Leave a finding you decide not
to fix unticked, with the reason after it. Add a test for every bug you
fix. Finish with the tests and lint clean.

## 9. Deploy

Follow `docs/deploy.md`.

# Intent: a secret cheat code

*From: Product. For: the games team. Change name: `cheat-code`.*

## Why

Tic-tac-toe has been live for a month. People play, but Hard can never be
beaten, and many players quit after two or three draws. Players love
secrets they can share with friends: we want a hidden cheat code that lets
you beat the computer once in a while. Players will pass the code around,
which brings them back to the page and brings their friends.

## What we want

- A secret code typed on the keyboard during a game against the computer
  unlocks a cheat for that game: the player may **steal** one square from
  the computer. The computer's mark on that square becomes the player's
  mark, and that counts as the player's move.
- One steal per game. It is never shown or hinted at on the page until the
  code has been typed. After that, the page makes clear how to use it.
- The code is the classic one: up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right,
  B, A.
- A game won with a steal is announced differently ("You won... with a
  little help"), and it is counted separately in the score. It must not
  count as a normal win.
- The cheat works only against the computer, at both levels, and not when
  two friends play on the same screen.

## What must not change

- Without the code, the game behaves exactly as it does today, and Hard
  still never loses to fair play.
- On the page, nobody can steal without typing the code. Nobody can steal
  twice in a game, even by sending requests to the server by hand.

## How we will know it worked

- It is live in production, the old game unchanged.
- People share the code: we see steals in games we did not set up ourselves.
# Spec: a secret cheat code (`cheat-code`)

Source: `changes/cheat-code/intent.md`. This is the design to build from.
It describes the change against the system as it is today
(`docs/architecture.md`, `tictactoe/`).

## Summary

Against the computer, typing ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A on the page unlocks a
**steal** for the current game: once per game the player may turn one of
the computer's O squares into an X, and that is the player's move. A win
that used a steal is announced as "You won... with a little help" and
counted in its own score column, never as a normal win.

The browser recognises the code and shows the steal controls. The server
judges every steal. To enforce "one steal per game" without keeping state,
the server signs each game position it hands out (an HMAC **game token**)
and accepts a steal only together with a valid token that says no steal has
been used. Requests without a token behave exactly as today.

## How it works today (the parts this change touches)

- A board is 9 cells, `"X"`, `"O"` or `""`. Whose turn it is follows from
  the counts: `game.turn()` is X when X count == O count. `game.validate()`
  accepts a board only if X count − O count is 0 or 1.
- `POST /api/move` takes the whole board, `cell`, `mode`, `level`. Against
  the computer the player is X and the board must have X to move. The server
  plays `cell`, then the computer's reply, and answers the new board.
- The server trusts nothing: any board that passes `validate()` is accepted.
  It has no idea whether that board came from a real game.
- The score (X wins, O wins, draws) lives in `app.js` until reload.

## New and changed rules

1. **Steal.** In a game against the computer, on the player's turn (X to
   move, game still playing), the player may name one cell that holds `"O"`.
   That cell becomes `"X"`. This is the player's move: the computer then
   replies as usual if the game goes on.
2. **Once per game.** A game has at most one steal. A game is one unbroken
   chain of positions handed out by the server, starting from the empty
   board (see "Game token").
3. **Only against the computer**, at both levels (`easy`, `hard`). Never in
   `friend` mode.
4. **Turn after a steal.** A steal changes a mark without adding one, so the
   counts no longer say whose turn it is. The rule becomes: with `s` steals
   used in the game (0 or 1), X is to move when X count − O count == `s`,
   otherwise O. A valid board has X count − O count equal to `s` or `s + 1`.
   With `s = 0` both rules are exactly today's.
5. **A steal can win at once.** If the stolen square completes a line of X,
   the game is won by X and the computer does not move. A steal never fills
   an empty square, so it cannot cause a draw by itself.
6. **Assisted win.** A game won by X in which a steal was used is an
   *assisted* win. The server says so in every answer (`assisted: true`).
   The page announces it as "You won... with a little help" and counts it
   only in the "With help" column, not in "X wins".
7. After a steal the game goes on normally: the computer (either level)
   plays its best/random move from the new position, and the computer can
   still win or draw. Those are counted as today (O win, draw).
8. **The code.** ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ ← → ← → B A (`ArrowUp ArrowUp ArrowDown ArrowDown
   ArrowLeft ArrowRight ArrowLeft ArrowRight b a`, B and A in either case).
   The code is recognised by the page only; it unlocks the steal controls
   for the current game. The server does not check the code (see Open
   questions 1).

## Game token (how the server enforces the rules without state)

The server keeps nothing between requests. Instead it signs what it must
trust when the browser sends it back, as `CLAUDE.md` allows.

- **Key.** `TICTACTOE_SECRET` from the environment (UTF-8 bytes) when set
  and not empty; otherwise 32 random bytes from `secrets.token_bytes` made
  once when the process starts. Production sets it through `ops/deploy.sh`
  and keeps it across releases, so tokens survive a deploy. The key is
  never logged, never sent, never put in an error message.
- **Format.** `"<s>.<mac>"`, where `<s>` is the number of steals used (`0`
  or `1`) and `<mac>` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the message
  `tictactoe-game-v1|<level>|<s>|<cells>`, with `<cells>` the 9 cells, each
  written as `X`, `O` or `-`. Example: `"0.3f9a…c1"` (64 hex digits).
  The token binds the board, the level and the steal count together;
  change any of them and it no longer verifies.
- **Checking.** Compare with `hmac.compare_digest`. A token that is not a
  string, has the wrong shape, an `<s>` other than `0`/`1`, or a MAC that
  does not match the request's `board` and `level` is rejected with
  `400 {"error": "the game token does not match this game"}`. This applies
  to any request that carries a `game` field, steal or not.
- **When the server hands one out** (the `game` field of the answer), only
  in `computer` mode and only while the game is still `playing`:
  - the request carried a valid token: the new position gets a token with
    the same `s` (or `s = 1` if this request was the steal);
  - the request had no token and its board was empty (first move of a new
    game): the new position gets a token with `s = 0`;
  - otherwise (no token, board not empty, e.g. a hand-made mid-game board
    or an older page): `game` is `null`. That game plays exactly as today
    and can never steal.
  So a token proves that the position was reached by legal moves through
  this server from an empty board, with `s` steals on the way.
- **Why this stops a second steal, even by hand.** A steal needs a token
  with `s = 0`. The answer to a steal only ever carries `s = 1` tokens, and
  every later answer in that game keeps `s = 1`. A board that has had a
  steal has X − O == 1 on X's turn, which no `s = 0` token can match and
  which `validate()` rejects without a token. Forging an `s = 0` token
  needs the key.
- **Replays.** Because the server is stateless, an old token stays valid.
  A player who kept an `s = 0` token from earlier in the same game can go
  back to that position and steal from there. That is a branch of the game
  (like an undo), and every branch still has at most one steal. Accepted
  (Open questions 3).

## API changes

`POST /api/move` keeps its path, limits (1024-byte body, 411, 413, 404,
405) and every existing field and error. New, all optional in the request:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `steal` | A cell 0–8 to steal, sent **instead of** `cell`. |
| `game` | The `game` token from the server's previous answer. |

New in every `200` answer (all modes):

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `game` | Token for the new position, or `null` (rules above). |
| `stealable` | Cells the player could steal now: the O cells when this answer has a token with `s = 0`, the game is playing and X is to move; otherwise `[]`. |
| `steal_used` | `true` once a steal has been used in this game (`s = 1`), else `false`. |
| `assisted` | `true` when `status` is `won`, `winner` is `X` and `steal_used` is `true`; else `false`. |

The page uses `stealable`, `steal_used` and `assisted` as given; it never
works out for itself which squares can be stolen or whether a win was
assisted.

### Examples (Hard; tokens shortened)

First move of a new game, no token (the existing request, unchanged):

```json
{"board": ["", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", ""], "cell": 0, "mode": "computer", "level": "hard"}
```

```json
{"board": ["X", "", "", "", "O", "", "", "", ""], "status": "playing",
 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 4,
 "game": "0.<64 hex>", "stealable": [4], "steal_used": false, "assisted": false}
```

Next move, sending the token back:

```json
{"board": ["X", "", "", "", "O", "", "", "", ""], "cell": 8, "mode": "computer",
 "level": "hard", "game": "0.<64 hex>"}
```

```json
{"board": ["X", "O", "", "", "O", "", "", "", "X"], "status": "playing",
 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 1,
 "game": "0.<64 hex>", "stealable": [1, 4], "steal_used": false, "assisted": false}
```

The steal: taking the centre completes the diagonal 0-4-8.

```json
{"board": ["X", "O", "", "", "O", "", "", "", "X"], "steal": 4, "mode": "computer",
 "level": "hard", "game": "0.<64 hex>"}
```

```json
{"board": ["X", "O", "", "", "X", "", "", "", "X"], "status": "won",
 "winner": "X", "line": [0, 4, 8], "turn": null, "computer_move": null,
 "game": null, "stealable": [], "steal_used": true, "assisted": true}
```

A steal that does not win (stealing cell 1 instead) gets the computer's
reply and an `s = 1` token; X is to move with X − O == 1. (Hard must block
row 0 at cell 2; this reply is the expected one, not recorded from code.)

```json
{"board": ["X", "X", "O", "", "O", "", "", "", "X"], "status": "playing",
 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 2,
 "game": "1.<64 hex>", "stealable": [], "steal_used": true, "assisted": false}
```

A friend game answers `game: null, stealable: [], steal_used: false,
assisted: false` in addition to today's fields.

### New errors (all `400 {"error": "..."}`)

Checked in this order, after today's checks of the body, `board` shape,
`mode` and `level`:

| Case | Message |
|------|---------|
| `game` present but not valid for this `board` and `level` (any request) | `the game token does not match this game` |
| both `cell` and `steal` present | `send either cell or steal, not both` |
| `steal` in `friend` mode | `you can only steal from the computer` |
| `steal` without `game` | `a steal needs the game token from the last answer` |
| `steal` with a token whose `s` is 1 | `you have already stolen a square in this game` |
| `steal` not a whole number 0–8 (`true` is not a number) | `steal must be a whole number from 0 to 8` |
| game already over | `the game is over` (today's message) |
| the cell is not an O (empty or X) | `you can only steal one of the computer's squares` |

The board check uses the token's `s`: a board with X − O outside
`s`..`s + 1` is rejected with today's message `X moves first and the
players alternate`, and with X − O ≠ `s` against the computer with today's
`against the computer you play X`.

## Logging (to see steals in production)

The intent will judge success by steals in games "we did not set up". The
server has no database, so after every successful steal the request handler
writes one line through `log_message` (stderr, which `ops/deploy.sh` sends
to `production/server.log`, next to the request line with the client
address):

```text
steal level=hard cell=4 status=won assisted=true
```

Nothing else is logged: no token, no key, no board. Because a steal needs a
token chain that started from an empty board, every logged steal happened
in a real game played through the server.

## The page

### Before the code (unchanged)

The page looks and behaves exactly as today: no steal button, no hint, no

exist in `index.html` with `hidden` and are not shown or announced.

### Recognising the code

- `app.js` listens to `keydown` on `document` and keeps the last 10 keys.
  When they equal the code, the code is typed. A sliding window means extra
  keys before it do not matter (↑ ↑ ↑ ↓ ↓ … still works).

  (`event.repeat`). Keys typed while focus is in a `<select>` are not
  recorded (arrows there change the mode or level, which starts a new game).
- The board's own arrow handling stays as it is: typing the code with the
  focus on the board moves the focus around, which is harmless; arrows never
  play a move.
- The code unlocks only when the mode is `computer` and the game is
  `playing`. Otherwise it does nothing at all (friend mode: no message, no
  hint).
- Unlocking lasts for the current game. A new game (button, mode or level
  change) locks it again; typing the code again unlocks it again.

### After the code

- The status line (`aria-live`) announces: "Cheat unlocked! Once this game,
  you may steal one of the computer's squares." The current status text

- A panel under the status line appears with a **Steal a square** button

- The score table shows a fourth column **With help** (and keeps showing it

## Open questions (with the decision taken)

1. **Should the server check the code?** No. The code is meant to be
   shared, so anyone sending requests by hand knows it anyway; making the
   browser send it would add nothing. "Nobody can steal without the code"
   is a promise about the page, kept by the page. The server enforces what
   it can: computer mode only, a real game, at most one steal.
2. **Phones and tablets without a keyboard?** Out of scope: the intent says
   "typed on the keyboard". No touch gesture is added. Product can ask for
   one as a separate change.
3. **Replaying an older token to steal in a different branch of the same
   game?** Allowed: it cannot be stopped without server state, and each
   branch still has at most one steal. Equivalent to starting over and
   replaying the same moves.
4. **Tokens for games already running when this ships?** Those pages run
   the old `app.js` and never send `game`; they play on as today and cannot
   steal. After a reload they get tokens.
5. **Development restarts.** Without `TICTACTOE_SECRET`, a restart makes a
   new key, so a game in progress gets 400 "the game token does not match"
   on its next move. Accepted for development; the page shows its usual
   error and New game fixes it. Production keeps its key across releases.
6. **Is an assisted win also an X win in the API?** Yes: `status: "won"`,
   `winner: "X"` as today, plus `assisted: true`. Only the page's score
   counts it separately. Keeps old clients and `status` unchanged.
7. **Can the computer still win after a steal?** Yes, and that is counted
   as a normal O win; a draw after a steal is a normal draw. Only X wins
   are "with help".
8. **Token after the game ends?** `null`: there is nothing left to play.
9. **Where the code lives in `app.js`.** Plain in the source. It is a
   shared secret by design; hiding it would be theatre.
# tictactoe

Tic-tac-toe for the website's games corner: a drawn 3x3 board in the
browser, against the computer (Easy or Hard, which never loses) or against
a friend on the same screen. The page keeps a running score and can be
played with the keyboard alone.

```bash
python3 -m tictactoe              # http://127.0.0.1:8000/
python3 -m tictactoe --port 0     # any free port; the URL is printed
python3 -m pytest -q              # unit and system tests
ruff check . && ruff format --check .
./ops/deploy.sh                   # to production, see docs/deploy.md
```

Python 3.12 or newer, standard library only.

## Documentation

- `docs/architecture.md`: modules, the move API, how the page works
- `docs/process.md`: how a change goes from intent to production
- `docs/deploy.md`: production and how to deploy to it
- `changes/<name>/`: one folder per change, with its intent, spec, plan,
  test report and review
# Architecture

```text
browser (static/)                          server (Python, stdlib)
┌───────────────────────┐  POST /api/move  ┌────────────────────────────┐
│ index.html  app.js    │ ───────────────▶ │ server.py  handle_move()   │
│ draws, sends clicks,  │    whole board   │   ├─ game.py  rules        │
│ keeps the score       │ ◀─────────────── │   └─ ai.py    computer     │
└───────────────────────┘   new board +    └────────────────────────────┘
                            outcome
```

The rules live in Python only. The browser never decides whether a move is
legal or who won: it shows what the server answers.

## Modules (`tictactoe/`)

| File | Job |
|------|-----|
| `game.py` | The rules. A board is a list of 9 cells, row by row, each `"X"`, `"O"` or `""`. X moves first, so `turn()` follows from the counts. `validate()` checks a board from outside, `play()` returns a new board (never changes its input) or raises `IllegalMoveError`, `outcome()` says `playing`, `won` (with winner and line) or `draw`. |
| `ai.py` | The computer. `choose_move(board, level)`: **hard** is negamax over the full game tree, cached, lowest cell among equals, so it is deterministic and never loses; **easy** takes a winning move if it sees one, otherwise plays at random. |
| `server.py` | `ThreadingHTTPServer`. Serves a fixed map of assets (no request path reaches the file system), `/health`, and the move API. Keeps no state. |
| `__main__.py` | `python3 -m tictactoe [--host] [--port]`; prints the URL it listens on. |
| `static/` | `index.html`, `style.css`, `app.js`. No build step, no libraries. |

## The move API

`POST /api/move`, a JSON body of at most 1024 bytes:

```json
{"board": ["X", "", "", "", "O", "", "", "", ""], "cell": 2, "mode": "computer", "level": "hard"}
```

- `mode` is `computer` (default) or `friend`; `level` is `easy` or `hard`
  (default), used only against the computer.
- Against the computer the player is always X, so the board must have X
  to move.
- The server plays `cell` for whoever is to move, then, against the
  computer and if the game goes on, the computer's reply as O.

Answer `200`:

```json
{"board": ["X", "", "X", "", "O", "", "", "", "O"], "status": "playing",
 "winner": null, "line": null, "turn": "X", "computer_move": 8}
```

`status` is `playing`, `won` or `draw`; `line` is the three winning cells;
`turn` is `null` once the game is over; `computer_move` is `null` when the
computer did not move.

Errors: `400 {"error": "..."}` for any bad input (bad JSON, impossible
board, taken square, game over, unknown mode or level), `411` without a
`Content-Length`, `413` for a body over 1024 bytes, `404` for other paths,
`405` for `GET /api/move`.

## The page

`app.js` holds the current answer from the server and the score (X wins, O
wins, draws, until the page is reloaded). Each click or Enter/Space on a
square sends one move. The board is one tab stop: arrow keys, Home and End
move between squares (roving `tabindex`), and every square has an
`aria-label` such as "Row 1, column 3, X, winning". The status line is an
`aria-live` region. Changing mode or level starts a new game.

## Tests

- `tests/test_game.py`, `tests/test_ai.py`, `tests/test_server.py`: unit

  as X and as O.
- `tests/system/test_http.py`: starts `python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` as a

## Phase 1: The rules and the signing key (no change to the API yet)

- [ ] `tictactoe/game.py`: add a keyword `steals=0` to `turn`, `validate` and
  `play`, following spec rule 4. X is to move when X count − O count ==
  `steals`, and a valid board has X − O equal to `steals` or `steals + 1`.
  With `steals=0`, every result, error message and the order of the checks
  stay exactly as they are today. `outcome()` and `legal_moves()` do not
  change.
- [ ] `tictactoe/game.py`: add `steal(board, cell, steals) -> list[str]`. It
  raises `IllegalMoveError` with the spec's exact messages, in the spec's
  order: `steals` already 1 ("you have already stolen a square in this
  game"), `cell` not a whole number 0–8 with `bool` refused ("steal must be a
  whole number from 0 to 8"), game over ("the game is over"), not X's turn
  under `steals` ("against the computer you play X"), cell not an `"O"`
  ("you can only steal one of the computer's squares"). It returns a new
  board with that cell set to `"X"` and never changes its input.
- [ ] `tictactoe/ai.py`: add a keyword `steals=0` to
  `choose_move(board, level, rng=None, *, steals=0)` and an argument to
  `best_move` and `value`, so the `@cache` key includes it. Pass it to every
  `game.turn`, `game.play` and recursive call, including Easy's check for a
  winning move. With `steals=0` the moves must be exactly today's.
- [ ] New `tictactoe/signing.py`, as the spec's "Game token" section
  describes. The key is `TICTACTOE_SECRET` encoded as UTF-8 when it is set
  and not empty, otherwise `secrets.token_bytes(32)`, made once at import.
  This is the only module that reads `os.environ`. `sign(board, level,
  steals)` returns `"<s>.<64 lowercase hex>"`: the HMAC-SHA256 of
  `tictactoe-game-v1|<level>|<s>|<cells>`, with each cell written as `X`,
  `O` or `-`. `verify(token, board, level) -> int` returns `s`. It raises
  `IllegalMoveError("the game token does not match this game")` when the
  token is not a `str`, does not have exactly the shape `0.`/`1.` followed
  by 64 lowercase hex digits, or has a MAC that does not match. It compares
  with `hmac.compare_digest`. The key never appears in a return value, an
  error or a log.
- [ ] `docs/architecture.md`, Modules table: describe the turn rule with
  `steals`, `game.steal`, `ai`'s `steals` argument and the new `signing.py`.
- [ ] Verify: `python3 -m pytest -q` passes with no test changed, and
  `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .` are clean. Then run a throwaway
  `python3` script, kept outside `tests/`. (a) It gets the committed code of
  commit `74dcd2d` with `git show 74dcd2d:tictactoe/<file>` into a temporary
  package. For every position reachable by legal play from the empty board,
  it checks that the new `turn`, `validate`, `play` and Hard
  `choose_move(..., steals=0)` match the old ones. It also checks that a set
  of impossible boards gets the same error message from both. (b) On the
  spec's board `X O _ / _ O _ / _ _ X`: `steal(…, 4, 0)` wins row/diagonal
  0-4-8. `steal(…, 1, 0)` gives `turn(…, steals=1) == "O"`, and Hard
  `choose_move(…, steals=1)` answers 2. Each `steal` error from task 2 has
  its exact message, and the input board is unchanged. (c) For
  `sign`/`verify`: a round trip returns `s`. A different board, a different
  level, a flipped `0.`/`1.` prefix, one changed hex digit, an uppercase MAC,
  a non-string and an empty string are all rejected. With
  `TICTACTOE_SECRET=abc` set, two separate processes make the same token.

2. **The move API judges steals.** `handle_move` reads the token and the steal and returns the four new fields. I wrote the phase 2 plan to `changes/cheat-code/plan.md`. It has four phases, each with 4–6 tasks, and ends with a `## For the preview` list. No code was changed and nothing is committed.

1. **The rules and the signing key**, with no API change yet. Adds a `steals` argument to the game rules and the computer player, adds `game.steal`, and adds a new `signing.py` that creates and checks the signed game token.
2. **The move API judges steals.** `handle_move` reads the token and the steal and returns the four new fields. It writes the `steal …` log line, which is what Product will use to see steals in games they did not set up. A request without a token goes through exactly today's checks, in today's order.
3. **The page carries the token.** `app.js` sends the token back with every move, and the new page elements are added but hidden, so nothing visible changes.
4. **The cheat on the page.** Recognising the code, the steal panel, steal mode, the new status messages and the "With help" score.

Each phase ends by running something: the existing tests, ruff, a throwaway Python script, and a real server on `--port 0` driven with `urllib`. Each phase also updates its part of `docs/architecture.md`, and leaves the game working.

**What you should know:**
- **"Old game unchanged" is checked against the old code.** Phases 1 and 2 load the code from commit `74dcd2d` with `git show` and compare it with the new code over every reachable position. `docs/process.md` only lists `python3` and `ruff` as verification tools, so this assumes `git` is also available, which it is in this repo.
- **Error order:** a request with no token keeps today's checks in today's order. Only requests that carry `game` or `steal` go through the spec's new order, so existing error messages can't change.
- **Browser-only checks are left to the preview.** That covers recognising the code, focus and screen-reader behaviour in steal mode, the 320 px layout, dark mode and whether the outline is clear without colour. The automated checks on the page only look at the served files and replay the requests `app.js` sends.
